title: Tail-Call Elimination and Rewriting Recursion as a Loop
quickIdea: A tail call needs no frame of its own, so a tail-recursive function can be rewritten as a loop with constant stack - but in C that is a compiler's choice, not a language guarantee.
remember: In a tail call the caller has nothing left to do, so the callee can return straight to the caller's caller and the frame can be replaced instead of stacked.
Tail-call elimination reduces stack space from O(n) to O(1) for a linear recursion: the same work with a constant number of frames.

In C it is an optimisation, not a promise. A compiler may do it at one optimisation level and not at another, and the standard requires nothing; a GATE answer that assumes constant stack for a tail-recursive C function is an assumption about the compiler.
The mechanical rewrite: parameters become loop variables, the base case becomes the loop condition, the recursive call becomes a back edge. factorial(n, acc) becomes a for loop over acc.

Recursion and iteration are equally powerful: any recursion can be simulated with an explicit stack, and any loop can be written as a recursion. The differences are constant factors, stack space and readability.
Choose recursion when the structure is a tree or a divide-and-conquer split; choose iteration when the structure is a sequence and the stack would only be carrying a counter.

example.prompt: Rewrite int fact(int n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * fact(n-1); } as a tail-recursive function and then as a loop.
example.work: Carry the product in a parameter: int fact2(int n, int acc) { return n <= 1 ? acc : fact2(n-1, acc*n); }. The call is now the last action, so the frame can be reused. The loop is int acc = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) acc *= i; - the parameter became the accumulator and the base case became the loop bound.
example.answer: fact2(n, 1) with the accumulator, and a single for loop; both use O(1) stack, while the original uses O(n).

gateAngle: GATE asks for space complexity, not for compiler behaviour, so the safe answer for a recursion whose frames still hold work is O(n) - as in GATE CSE 2005 Q.81(a), where every frame adds to sum after the call returns. Only a genuine tail call can honestly be called O(1), and only with a note that it depends on the compiler.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: The recursive foo of GATE CSE 2005 Q.81(a) adds to sum after each call. Why is its space not O(1) even though the calls look like a loop?
variations.answer: Because each frame is still holding a partial sum and a return address when the next call is made; the additions happen on the unwinding, so the frames cannot be reused.
variations.why: The distinction between a loop-shaped recursion and a tail call, tested through the space complexity.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is return n * fact(n-1) not a tail call?
variations.answer: Because the multiplication happens after the call returns: the frame must stay alive to perform it. A tail call returns the callee's result unchanged.
variations.why: The single most common misreading of 'the call is the last thing in the function'.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A tail-recursive function is compiled without optimisation. What is its space complexity?
variations.answer: O(n) in practice, because the frames are stacked; the O(1) figure requires tail-call elimination.
variations.why: GATE has never required the compiler-dependent answer, and this variation is exactly why.

trap.what: Assuming the C compiler always eliminates tail calls, and answering O(1) stack for any recursive function.
trap.why: C has no such guarantee. Optimisation level, calling convention and whether the call is really in tail position all change the outcome, and a paper that wanted O(1) would have to say so.
trap.counterexample: gcc compiles fact2 without elimination at -O0, so fact2(100000) overflows the stack even though the call is in tail position.

check.question: int s(int n, int acc) { return n == 0 ? acc : s(n-1, acc+n); } How many frames are alive at the deepest point, and how many would be if the addition were written after the call?
check.answer: One frame if the compiler eliminates the tail call, otherwise n+1; and n+1 in both cases for the version that adds after the call.
check.explanation: Only a call in tail position can reuse its frame, and only when the compiler chooses to do so.

visual.title: Recursion
covers: a recursive definition: smaller copy plus a base case
one frame per call: own parameters, own locals, own return address
nothing is computed on the way down; values combine on the way up
fact(n) and sumTo(n): calls = depth = n+1
the C standard does not require tail call optimisation
static local inside a recursion is one object shared by all frames
GATE 2011 foo(n, r) is the base-r digit sum; foo(513,2) = 2
